Dear Vandana,

I did something this week I've been avoiding for a year. I admitted medicine might not be for me.

You know how hard I've worked at chemistry. Tuitions, extra notes, two hours every evening. And my last three tests were 41, 38 and 44. Steady effort, steady failure. I kept telling myself it would click.

On Monday I went to the school counsellor. I expected her to say try harder. Instead she asked what I actually enjoyed in class. I said maths, especially statistics, and that I'd been avoiding it because everyone tells me "a girl like you, good at science, should become a doctor".

She showed me what data and statistics courses look like. I sat in her room and felt, for the first time in months, curious instead of scared.

I'm shifting my focus. It feels strange and a bit sad, but also like breathing out.

Gopika

You're asking me if it's okay to change your mind, Shalini? I changed mine in the middle of Class 11. Let me tell you how.

I'm Parul. I'd wanted to be a doctor since I was eight. My whole family was proud. So in Class 11, I studied chemistry every single evening. Two hours. Tuition on Saturdays. And my tests came back 40, 42, 39. Not because I was lazy. I just wasn't getting it.

One day I cried in the washroom after a test and my class teacher sent me to the counsellor. I was ashamed to say it out loud, but I did: "Maybe medicine isn't for me."

She didn't argue. She asked what I liked. Statistics, I said. The one chapter in maths I always finished first. She showed me data science programmes. I'd been avoiding that idea for a year because it felt like giving up.

It wasn't giving up. It was steering.
